To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the age- related decrease in femoral bone strength is associated with both secondary hyperpar- athyroidism and skeletal anabolic growth factor deficiency in elderly women.
the age-related bone loss in the femoral neck is associated with both secondary hyperparathryroidism and skeletal IGF-I deficiency.

age- related bone mass decline in the proximal human femur is associated with secondary hyperparathy- ridism, and that the skeletal content of growth factors such as IGF- I decreases in cortical bone with age, implying a possible contribution of skeletal growth factor deficiency to the age- associated loss of femoral bone mass.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathogenesis and prevention of age- related osteoporosis.
the elucidation of the mechanisms that contribute to age- related bone remodeling.
the mechanisms of age- related bone mass decline and osteoporosis in the elderly.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
age- related bone mass loss in the elderly is caused by both hyperparathyroid- ism- mediated bone resorption and skeletal growth factor defi- ciency.
the age- related decline in bone strength is the net result of both increased bone resorption and decreased bone formation, the latter probably related to growth factor deficiency.
both secondary hyperpar- athyroidism and skeletal IGF- 1 deficiency may be implicated in senile osteoporotic hip fracture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pathophysiology of age- related bone mass loss and hip fracture risk in elderly women is multifactorial, involving both secondary hyperpar- athyroidism and skeletal IGF- 1 deficiency.
the age- related loss in femoral bone mass may be caused by a combination of vitamin D deficiency and growth factor deficiency.

age- related bone mass loss is the result of an imbalance between the rate of bone formation and the rate of bone resorption, and this imbalance is due to a combination of both secondary hyperparathryroidism and skeletal IGF-1 deficiency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
age- related bone mass loss is a complex multifactorial phenomenon.
the age- related decrease in skeletal growth factors is a novel finding that may be of relevance to our understanding of the pathogenesis of senile osteoporo- sis.
age- related bone remodeling is not a simple function of vitamin D status.
